chunks: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Qasim from al-Nakha'i from Safwan ibn Yahya from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
When you slaughter or sacrifice, eat and feed, as Allah the Exalted said: 'So eat of it and feed the contented and the beggar.'

He explained: 'The contented is the one who is content with what you give him; the beggar is the one who clings to you; the petitioner is the one who asks you with his hands; and the wretched is the poor man.'

key_terms.السَّائِلُ: the petitioner (one who asks, often with hands extended)
key_terms.الْقَانِعُ: the contented one (who accepts charity gracefully without excessive asking)
key_terms.الْمُعْتَرُّ: the beggar/clinger (one who clings to people for sustenance)
key_terms.نَحَرَ: to sacrifice (specifically camels, or generally to slaughter)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the contented and the beggar in Islamic charity etiquette?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the Quranic command to distribute meat by defining the recipients: 'al-qani' refers to one who is content with what is given, while 'al-mu'tarr' denotes the beggar who clings or asks persistently. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on balancing generosity with the dignity of the recipient, encouraging owners to feed both the self-sufficient poor and those actively seeking sustenance.
